dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation

evidence.note: Inspected workspace/data/GPU, read the 240-line template (recognized it as data-loading only), identified .bin shard sizes, the 32MB cap, tied-embedding checkpoint implications, and picked load_model_for_verification as the loading path.

Repeatedly admitted the bpb conversion was a 'rough guess' from an assumed bytes/token constant — the size/capacity/bpb design envelope was not derived up front, weakening orientation for most of the run.

Ran a verification script confirming file size, module import, loader path, and the forward/loss=cross_entropy contract; probed the actual SentencePiece tokenizer to compute real bytes/token for bpb — genuine data/tokenizer probing rather than guessing.

Only after a completed 14k-iter run discovered the loaded/dequantized checkpoint (2.82) was far worse than in-memory (2.667) due to int4 quantization — the dequant round-trip, a core contract element the grader actually scores, was learned reactively, not front-loaded.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the spec and template, correctly identified shard format, vocab, the 32MB cap, chose one loading path, understood both forward signatures, verified the loss contract, and probed the real tokenizer — comfortably exceeding the level-5 anchor. However it fell short of level 8's deliberate full-contract mapping: the decisive int8/int4 dequant round-trip degradation was discovered late (step 104) rather than reasoned up front, and the bpb envelope stayed a stated 'rough guess' through most of the trajectory. That reactive-rather-than-anticipatory grasp of the quantization contract places it at a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition

evidence.note: Wrote a full training script then launched a full-scale 37.4M/9000-iter run in one shot, hoping it would train, fit, and pass — a monolithic first push rather than a tiny end-to-end baseline.

First checkpoint at iter 500 had a size done-check (28.73 MB under cap), showing a rough per-eval size criterion, but this emerged from the production run, not a deliberate de-risking baseline milestone.
Contract load/forward verification and the first real bpb estimate happened only AFTER the full 10k-iter run — correctness verification deferred rather than gated before scaling.

Scaled to a 60.8M int4 model and ran the full 14k iters plus continuations before ever checking dequantized-load fidelity; at step 104 discovered loaded loss (2.82) vastly worse than in-memory (2.667) — the key correctness gate was missed until huge compute was spent.

A long series of re-quantization retries (mixed, group-128, group-32) chasing a quantization gap that a baseline-first end-to-end load-and-score check would have caught early — evidence scaling and correctness were entangled, not sequenced.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed implicit ordering (build→train→quantize→verify→submit) with a continuous size done-check and a rough val-loss target, which lifts it above pure anchor-3 monolithic behavior. But it never established a deliberate tiny-model end-to-end baseline before scaling, and the decisive dequant-fidelity/contract gates were verified only after full-scale runs, so capacity scaling and correctness stayed entangled — well short of the explicit, contract-and-size-locked-before-scaling milestones of anchor 8. This places it between anchors 3 and 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification

evidence.note: Ran dedicated verification script: file size < cap, imported train_AGENT.py, loaded checkpoint through loader path, confirmed forward/loss contract, and computed accurate local bpb from tokenizer bytes/token (not the script's rough estimate).

Grader-faithful catch: verified the loaded/dequantized int4 checkpoint and found loaded val_loss 2.8198 vs in-memory 2.667 — detected quantization round-trip degradation, the exact silent failure this dimension targets.
Comparative round-trip experiments (group32, mixed int8/int4) on temp files, measuring loaded validation for each encoding before committing — near-harness verification behavior.
Final gate before submission: confirmed 30.6MB < 32MB cap, loader path works, logits shape correct, and loss matches cross-entropy exactly.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly reloaded the checkpoint through its own loader/dequant path, confirmed the byte cap, computed loaded local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy, and explicitly asserted the cross-entropy/logits forward contract — and crucially caught the int4 dequant round-trip degradation (in-memory vs loaded gap), which is the signature level-8 behavior of grader-faithful self-verification. It falls short of level 10 because verification was run as manual milestone checks rather than a single reusable automated gate on every iteration, and it did not secure explicit margin against the threshold. This places it firmly at the level-8 anchor.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking

evidence.note: Established a 500-iter eval cadence on the val proxy from the start, reported checkpoint size + val_loss each time, and immediately related it to the target ('need val_loss ~2.28/2.3').

Tracked val trajectory point-by-point across the run, computed slope ('~0.01 per 500'), extrapolated whether the pace would cross ~2.64, and compared the large model's curve against the earlier small model at matching iterations.
Stopped the fine-tune based on a read (val 2.7749 worse than prior 2.7582) rather than a fixed step count — a divergence/no-progress detection driving a course change.
Discovered the loaded/dequantized val (2.82) was ~0.14 worse than the in-memory val (2.667) — an important monitoring insight, but only measured post-hoc, never tracked during training.
Repeatedly recognized plateaus (val stalling at ~2.67-2.71, no-save events) and reasoned about diminishing returns.

End-stage thrash: group32/mixed re-encoding experiments overwrote the best checkpoint and it submitted a checkpoint (loaded bpb ~1.05) worse than earlier discarded candidates — imperfect done-vs-remaining tracking.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a continuous, quantitative picture of the val trajectory vs the target and remaining compute across many runs, detected plateaus, and made stop/continue/change decisions from that read rather than fixed step counts (steps 44-88, 54, 129) — squarely level 8. It fell short of level 10 because its target picture stayed fuzzy for most of the run (rough bpb conversion), the score-determining loaded-checkpoint metric was only measured after runs, and it ground saturated configs and thrashed at the end, overwriting and ultimately submitting a worse checkpoint (steps 104, 157, 165-172).

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints

evidence.note: First run failed on torch.compile (missing C compiler) and 37.4M params too big for cap; diagnosed both, disabled compile, dropped tied lm_head, shrank to ~31M. Then OOM at batch 256 → reasoned single-lever reduction to 128. Targeted cause-based fixes, not random tweaks.

Fine-tune resume worsened val (2.776 vs 2.758); recognized it as a dead end, abandoned it, and reframed around the unused byte budget (28.6/32MB) to train a larger 60.8M int4 model — capacity-vs-size reasoning.

Key binding-constraint diagnosis: loaded int4 val (2.82) >> in-memory (2.667) identified quantization loss (not capacity/optimization) as the limiter; used 7.6MB headroom to move to mixed int8/int4 — trades quant scheme against accuracy within the cap (anchor-8).
Diagnosed per-row int4 scales as too coarse and switched to groupwise int4 (scales every 128), refining the quantization design against the byte budget.

Diagnosed that re-encoding an already-quantized static model can't recover accuracy; adapted to a fresh short fine-tune before group32 encoding — but these late experiments were partly redundant dead-ends pursued after weak evidence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed the actual binding constraint from evidence — compile/size, OOM, capacity underuse, and most importantly the in-memory-vs-loaded quantization gap — and adapted the design accordingly, explicitly trading depth/width against the quantization scheme within the byte cap, which matches the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because the decisive quant-loss diagnosis came only after a full 14k-iter run (sunk compute), it lost its earlier int8 checkpoint during a detour, and the closing group32/mixed re-encoding attempts were partly redundant dead-ends rather than early-abandoned, so corrections were compounding but not the clean frontier optimization of the top anchor.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation

evidence.note: Checked GPU/data and sized the model (~30M params) explicitly to fit the 32MB checkpoint budget — goal-oriented run sizing, an element of anchor 5.

Committed directly to a full 10k-iteration run (est. ~45 min) with no cheap smoke-test/probe first; used quick OOM crashes to fix batch size and checked checkpoint size at first eval — partial cheap validation but no pre-commit end-to-end probe.
Scaled to a 60.8M int4 model for a full 14k-iter run (~50 min) chosen by intuition rather than a probe estimating steps/capacity needed to cross the threshold.

Only after the entire 14k int4 run did it discover the loaded/dequantized loss was badly degraded (2.667→2.82). No cheap quantization round-trip probe beforehand — a major budget-allocation waste of the main run.

Chained multiple full-length recovery continuations (mixed 8k, group128 6k, group32 2k), each run to its scheduled end despite plateaus, with no upfront phase-budget plan and no reserved margin — reactive 'spend whatever the run takes' behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows partial goal-sizing (fitting the checkpoint budget, estimating ~45-50 min runs) and some cheap validation (OOM batch tuning, post-run contract checks), which lifts it above pure anchor-3, but it never runs informative probes to estimate steps/capacity needed and, critically, failed to reserve cheap compute to validate the quantized-load path before spending the entire int4 main budget on a broken encoding (step 104). Run lengths were chosen by intuition and executed to completion despite plateaus, with no upfront cross-phase allocation or reserved margin, so it falls short of anchor 5's 'reserves cheap compute for contract validation before committing' and well short of anchor 8. This lands at a 4, between reactive spending (3) and disciplined goal-sizing (5).

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train an LM on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit an int8-compressed checkpoint (≤32 MB decimal) that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty is multi-source: an exact and dual-path loading/forward contract that silently fails the grade if mismatched, a hard size budget coupled to model capacity via quantization, training convergence under implicit compute limits, and a local val_bpb proxy that must be trusted and monitored. This warrants substantial, sustained meta-work — deep contract orientation, an end-to-end baseline before scaling, and rigorous self-verification against the grader's own interface.

dimensions.name: Contract & environment orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the loading/forward contract, data format (.bin shards, tokenizer), size budget, and template before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads via one of two specific interfaces and calls forward with two exact signatures; a checkpoint that trains perfectly but violates the contract or size cap scores zero. Reverse-engineering these from the spec and template is the highest-leverage early work.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no reading of the template, data format, tokenizer, or the loading/forward contract; assumes defaults.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; aware there is a size limit and a val target but hazy on the exact load path or the dual forward signature.
anchors.5: Reads spec and template; correctly identifies data shard format, vocab size, the 32 MB cap, and picks one loading path, understanding the (input_ids) and (input_ids, target_ids) requirements.
anchors.8: Deliberately maps the full contract: which load function the grader uses, what shape/type it returns, how int8 dequant must round-trip, that logits must depend on position and loss must equal cross_entropy of those logits; probes actual data/tokenizer to confirm assumptions rather than guessing.
anchors.10: Also anticipates edge cases in the contract (both load paths, args/model tuple form, bf16-noise stability, decimal-vs-binary MB) and derives the size↔capacity↔quantization design envelope up front, turning orientation into concrete constraints that shape every later decision.

dimensions.name: Baseline-first decomposition
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered milestones — a working end-to-end pipeline before scaling — each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Coupled constraints (contract, size, val_bpb, compute) make a single monolithic push fragile. Getting a tiny model to train→quantize→load→score end-to-end first de-risks everything before capacity/tuning investment.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated push: launch a big training run hoping it trains, fits, loads, and passes all at once.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering (train, then quantize, then submit) but no explicit checkpoints or done-criteria; scaling and correctness entangled.
anchors.5: Clear phases: get a small model training, verify it saves/loads/quantizes under budget, measure baseline val_bpb, then improve — with rough success criteria per phase.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete gate (loads via grader interface / size < 32MB / forward contract holds / val_bpb measured), sequenced so contract+size correctness is locked before capacity scaling and tuning.
anchors.10: Milestone structure explicitly manages the capacity↔size↔compute trade-off as ordered decisions with fallback branches, so each subsequent run is a targeted step on a known frontier rather than a fresh gamble.

dimensions.name: Grader-faithful verification
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond training loss: that the checkpoint loads via the grader's own interface, fits the byte cap, satisfies both forward signatures, and dequantizes correctly.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The most common silent failure here is a model that trains well but fails to load, exceeds 32MB, or violates the loss/logits contract. Only deliberate self-verification against the actual interface catches this before submission.

anchors.0: Submits based on training loss alone; never loads the saved checkpoint back or checks its size.
anchors.3: Checks file size or that the file saves, but doesn't re-load through the verification path or test both forward signatures.
anchors.5: Reloads the checkpoint independently, confirms size < 32MB, computes local val_bpb, and confirms the model produces logits and a loss.
anchors.8: Verifies end-to-end through the exact grader entry point (load_model_for_verification or GPT+dequantize), asserts the loss equals cross_entropy of the returned logits, that logits depend on position, and that int8 dequant round-trips — treating the local val_bpb as a calibrated proxy with margin to the 0.983 threshold.
anchors.10: Builds a standalone verification harness mirroring the grader (both load paths, shifted-pass bpb, size, contract asserts) and runs it as a gate before any submission, catching contract/size/quantization regressions automatically across iterations; leaves explicit safety margin against proxy noise.

dimensions.name: Training & budget progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb trajectory vs the target and of compute spent vs remaining, detecting divergence, overfitting, or plateaus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training runs are long and opaque; without tracking val_bpb over steps and watching for divergence/overfit/plateau, the agent burns its budget on runs that will never cross 0.983 or silently regress.

anchors.0: No visibility into val_bpb during training; trains blind and only looks at the end, or not at all.
anchors.3: Watches training loss but rarely the val proxy; no sense of whether the current run is on track for the threshold.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during/after runs and compares to the 0.983 target, noticing gross problems like divergence or no improvement.
anchors.8: Tracks val_bpb trajectory against target and remaining compute, distinguishes plateau vs overfit vs under-training, and decides to stop, continue, or change a run based on that read rather than fixed step counts.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate done-vs-remaining model across many runs — recognizing diminishing returns, near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and thrash — and reallocates effort deliberately instead of grinding a saturated configuration.

dimensions.name: Course-correction under constraints
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, quantization, hyperparameters, or plan when a run diverges, overshoots the size cap, or fails to approach the target.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts routinely miss on size or bpb; progress depends on diagnosing WHY (too big, under-capacity, bad LR, quant loss) and changing the right lever rather than repeating the same run.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or ignores a size/contract failure and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with undirected tweaks (nudge LR, shrink randomly) without diagnosing the cause.
anchors.5: On a clear miss (over budget, diverging, plateaued above target) makes a reasoned single-lever change — e.g. adjust dims to fit, change LR, tune training length — and re-checks.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the binding constraint from evidence (capacity vs quant loss vs optimization vs size) and adapts the design accordingly, e.g. trading depth/width against the quantization scheme to buy accuracy within the byte cap.
anchors.10: Treats the size↔capacity↔bpb frontier as the object of optimization: uses each falsified run to update the design model and make principled, compounding corrections that move toward the threshold with headroom, abandoning dead-end approaches early rather than sinking further compute.

dimensions.name: Compute/time budget allocation
dimensions.description: Deciding how to spend limited training compute/wall-clock across baseline validation, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning.
dimensions.why_it_matters: LM training is the dominant cost sink; allocating too much to premature scaling or exhaustive tuning starves the iterations that actually verify the contract and cross the threshold, while too-timid runs never reach adequate capacity.

anchors.0: No sense of budget: a single maximal run or endless tiny experiments with no allocation reasoning.
anchors.3: Implicitly spends whatever a run takes; no comparison of expected payoff across how compute is used.
anchors.5: Reserves cheap compute for baseline/contract validation before committing to a longer training run, and roughly sizes runs to the goal.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget across phases — cheap end-to-end validation, a right-sized main run, targeted tuning — and adjusts allocation as results come in.
anchors.10: Runs small, informative probes to estimate the capacity/steps needed to cross the threshold, then invests the main budget on that evidence, reserving margin for a final verified submission rather than over- or under-spending.
